excerpts.markdown: (1) $d$ which merely means “a little bit of.”
excerpts.why: It gives the learner the plain-language meaning of the d symbol before any notation is used.

excerpts.location: To deliver you from the Preliminary Terrors
excerpts.latex: Thus $\ds\int dx$ means the sum of all the little bits of~$x$; or $\ds\int dt$ means the sum of all the little bits of~$t$.
excerpts.markdown: Thus $\ds\int dx$ means the sum of all the little bits of $x$; or $\ds\int dt$ means the sum of all the little bits of $t$.
excerpts.why: It pairs the integral sign with the differential so the learner reads an integral as adding up little bits.

excerpts.location: To deliver you from the Preliminary Terrors
excerpts.latex: The word ``integral'' simply means ``the whole.''
excerpts.markdown: The word “integral” simply means “the whole.”
excerpts.why: It explains the name integral in common terms, so the word no longer seems mysterious.

excerpts.location: To deliver you from the Preliminary Terrors
excerpts.latex: Thus $dx$ means a little bit of~$x$; or $du$ means a little bit of~$u$. Ordinary mathematicians think it more polite to say ``an element of,'' instead of ``a little bit of.'' Just as you please.
excerpts.markdown: Thus $dx$ means a little bit of $x$; or $du$ means a little bit of $u$. Ordinary mathematicians think it more polite to say “an element of,” instead of “a little bit of.” Just as you please.
excerpts.why: It gives the plain meaning of d and says the formal wording is optional.

excerpts.location: To deliver you from the Preliminary Terrors
excerpts.latex: If you think of the duration of time for one hour, you may (if you like) think of it as cut up into $3600$ little bits called seconds. The whole of the $3600$ little bits added up together make one hour.
excerpts.markdown: If you think of the duration of time for one hour, you may (if you like) think of it as cut up into $3600$ little bits called seconds. The whole of the $3600$ little bits added up together make one hour.
excerpts.why: A familiar example of little bits adding up to a whole.

excerpts.location: To deliver you from the Preliminary Terrors
excerpts.latex: \First{The} preliminary terror, which chokes off most fifth-form boys from even attempting to learn how to calculate, can be abolished once for all by simply stating what is the meaning---in common-sense terms---of the two principal symbols that are used in calculating.
excerpts.markdown: The preliminary terror, which chokes off most fifth-form boys from even attempting to learn how to calculate, can be abolished once for all by simply stating what is the meaning---in common-sense terms---of the two principal symbols that are used in calculating.
excerpts.why: It names the fear of calculus and promises to remove it by explaining the two symbols in plain terms.

excerpts.location: To deliver you from the Preliminary Terrors
excerpts.latex: Now any fool can see that if $x$~is considered as made up of a lot of little bits, each of which is called~$dx$, if you add them all up together you get the sum of all the~$dx$'s, (which is the same thing as the whole of~$x$). The word ``integral'' simply means ``the whole.''
excerpts.markdown: Now any fool can see that if $x$ is considered as made up of a lot of little bits, each of which is called $dx$, if you add them all up together you get the sum of all the $dx$’s, (which is the same thing as the whole of $x$). The word “integral” simply means “the whole.”
excerpts.why: It shows that the integral is the whole obtained by adding up the little bits.

excerpts.location: To deliver you from the Preliminary Terrors
excerpts.latex: When you see an expression that begins with this terrifying symbol, you will henceforth know that it is put there merely to give you instructions that you are now to perform the operation (if you can) of totalling up all the little bits that are indicated by the symbols that follow. That's all.
excerpts.markdown: When you see an expression that begins with this terrifying symbol, you will henceforth know that it is put there merely to give you instructions that you are now to perform the operation (if you can) of totalling up all the little bits that are indicated by the symbols that follow. That’s all.
excerpts.why: It tells the learner the integral sign is only an instruction to add up little bits, which takes the fear out of it.

excerpts.latex: Obviously $1$~minute is a very small quantity of time compared with a whole week.
excerpts.markdown: Obviously $1$ minute is a very small quantity of time compared with a whole week.
excerpts.why: Shows through a familiar example that smallness is relative, which is the chapter's central point.

excerpts.latex:
The mathematicians talk about the second order of ``magnitude''
  (\IE~greatness) when they really mean second order of \emph{smallness}.
  This is very confusing to beginners.
excerpts.markdown: The mathematicians talk about the second order of “magnitude” (*i.e.* greatness) when they really mean second order of *smallness*. This is very confusing to beginners.
excerpts.why: Warns learners about a common source of confusion in the wording used by mathematicians.

excerpts.latex: But, it must be remembered, that small quantities if they occur in our expressions as factors multiplied by some other factor, may become important if the other factor is itself large. Even a farthing becomes important if only it is multiplied by a few hundred.
excerpts.markdown: But, it must be remembered, that small quantities if they occur in our expressions as factors multiplied by some other factor, may become important if the other factor is itself large. Even a farthing becomes important if only it is multiplied by a few hundred.
excerpts.why: Cautions that smallness is relative and a small quantity multiplied by a large one may not be negligible.

excerpts.latex: Then we see that the smaller a small quantity itself is, the more negligible does the corresponding small quantity of the second order become.
excerpts.markdown: Then we see that the smaller a small quantity itself is, the more negligible does the corresponding small quantity of the second order become.
excerpts.why: States the key reason higher-order small quantities can be dropped.

excerpts.latex: Nowadays we call these small quantities of the second order of smallness ``seconds.'' But few people know \emph{why} they are so called.
excerpts.markdown: Nowadays we call these small quantities of the second order of smallness “seconds.” But few people know *why* they are so called.
excerpts.why: Shows that the familiar word 'second' comes from 'second order of smallness', which makes the idea of orders concrete.

excerpts.latex: Now in the calculus we write $dx$ for a little bit of~$x$. These things such as~$dx$, and~$du$, and~$dy$, are called ``differentials,'' the differential of~$x$, or of~$u$, or of~$y$, as the case may be.
excerpts.markdown: Now in the calculus we write $dx$ for a little bit of $x$. These things such as $dx$, and $du$, and $dy$, are called “differentials,” the differential of $x$, or of $u$, or of $y$, as the case may be.
excerpts.why: Introduces differential notation as 'a little bit of' a quantity.

excerpts.latex: Let us think of $x$ as a quantity that can grow by a small amount so as to become $x + dx$, where $dx$~is the small increment added by growth. The square of this is $x^2 + 2x · dx + (dx)^2$.
excerpts.markdown: Let us think of $x$ as a quantity that can grow by a small amount so as to become $x + dx$, where $dx$ is the small increment added by growth. The square of this is $x^2 + 2x · dx + (dx)^2$.
excerpts.why: Sets up the worked example that separates first-order and second-order terms.

excerpts.latex: Clearly $(dx)^2$ is negligible if only we consider the increment~$dx$ to be itself small enough.
excerpts.markdown: Clearly $(dx)^2$ is negligible if only we consider the increment $dx$ to be itself small enough.
excerpts.why: Gives the conclusion of the growing-square picture: the tiny corner square can be ignored.

excerpts.latex: An ox might worry about a flea of ordinary size---a small creature of the first order of smallness. But he would probably not trouble himself about a flea's flea; being of the second order of smallness, it would be negligible.
excerpts.markdown: An ox might worry about a flea of ordinary size---a small creature of the first order of smallness. But he would probably not trouble himself about a flea’s flea; being of the second order of smallness, it would be negligible.
excerpts.why: A humorous analogy that makes orders of smallness easy to remember.

excerpts.latex: Those which we regard as of fixed value, and call \emph{constants}, we generally denote algebraically by letters from the beginning of the alphabet, such as $a$,~$b$, or~$c$; while those which we consider as capable of growing, or (as mathematicians say) of ``varying,'' we denote by letters from the end of the alphabet, such as $x$,~$y$,~$z$, $u$,~$v$,~$w$, or sometimes~$t$.
excerpts.markdown: Those which we regard as of fixed value, and call *constants*, we generally denote algebraically by letters from the beginning of the alphabet, such as $a$, $b$, or $c$; while those which we consider as capable of growing, or (as mathematicians say) of “varying,” we denote by letters from the end of the alphabet, such as $x$, $y$, $z$, $u$, $v$, $w$, or sometimes $t$.
excerpts.why: Gives the learner the basic split between fixed and varying quantities and the lettering habit that goes with it.

excerpts.latex: Suppose the ladder was so long that when the bottom end~$A$ was $19$~inches from the wall the top end~$B$ reached just $15$~feet from the ground. Now, if you were to pull the bottom end out $1$~inch more, how much would the top end come down?
excerpts.markdown: Suppose the ladder was so long that when the bottom end $A$ was $19$ inches from the wall the top end $B$ reached just $15$ feet from the ground. Now, if you were to pull the bottom end out $1$ inch more, how much would the top end come down?
excerpts.why: Poses a concrete ladder problem in which a positive step in x gives a negative step in y, and the answer is then worked out in numbers.

excerpts.latex: It is a solemn scientific name for this very simple thing. But we are not going to be frightened by solemn names, when the things themselves are so easy.
excerpts.markdown: It is a solemn scientific name for this very simple thing. But we are not going to be frightened by solemn names, when the things themselves are so easy.
excerpts.why: Eases a learner's fear of the term differential coefficient with the author's cheerful impatience for long names.

excerpts.latex: You have now to learn to go hunting in a new way; the fox being now neither $x$ nor~$y$. Instead of this you have to hunt for this curious cub called~$\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
excerpts.markdown: You have now to learn to go hunting in a new way; the fox being now neither $x$ nor $y$. Instead of this you have to hunt for this curious cub called $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
excerpts.why: Contrasts the school-algebra hunt for an unknown with the new hunt for a ratio, in a charming old image.

excerpts.latex: We classify all quantities into two classes: \emph{constants} and \emph{variables}. Those which we regard as of fixed value, and call \emph{constants}, we generally denote algebraically by letters from the beginning of the alphabet, such as $a$,~$b$, or~$c$; while those which we consider as capable of growing, or (as mathematicians say) of ``varying,'' we denote by letters from the end of the alphabet, such as $x$,~$y$,~$z$, $u$,~$v$,~$w$, or sometimes~$t$.
excerpts.markdown: We classify all quantities into two classes: *constants* and *variables*. Those which we regard as of fixed value, and call *constants*, we generally denote algebraically by letters from the beginning of the alphabet, such as $a$, $b$, or $c$; while those which we consider as capable of growing, or (as mathematicians say) of “varying,” we denote by letters from the end of the alphabet, such as $x$, $y$, $z$, $u$, $v$, $w$, or sometimes $t$.
excerpts.why: It gives the learner the basic split between fixed letters and growing letters that the whole calculus rests on.

excerpts.latex: So we see that making $dx$ an increase of $1$~inch has resulted in making $dy$ a decrease of $0.11$~inch.
excerpts.markdown: So we see that making $dx$ an increase of $1$ inch has resulted in making $dy$ a decrease of $0.11$ inch.
excerpts.why: It states in plain words what a pair of small changes in a ladder problem means, which a learner can check with numbers.

excerpts.latex: For example $x^2 + 3 = 2y - 7$ is an implicit function in $x$~and~$y$; it may be written $y = \dfrac{x^2 + 10}{2}$ (explicit function of~$x$) or $x = \sqrt{2y - 10}$ (explicit function of~$y$).
excerpts.markdown: For example $x^2 + 3 = 2y - 7$ is an implicit function in $x$ and $y$; it may be written $y = \dfrac{x^2 + 10}{2}$ (explicit function of $x$) or $x = \sqrt{2y - 10}$ (explicit function of $y$).
excerpts.why: A single worked equation shows how the same relation can be read as an implicit or an explicit function.

excerpts.latex: Now right through the differential calculus we are hunting, hunting, hunting for a curious thing, a mere ratio, namely, the proportion which $dy$~bears to~$dx$ when both of them are indefinitely small.
excerpts.markdown: Now right through the differential calculus we are hunting, hunting, hunting for a curious thing, a mere ratio, namely, the proportion which $dy$ bears to $dx$ when both of them are indefinitely small.
excerpts.why: States in one vivid sentence what the whole differential calculus is after.

excerpts.latex: If, while $x$ is, as before, the distance of the foot of the ladder from the wall, $y$~is, instead of the height reached, the horizontal length of the wall, or the number of bricks in it, or the number of years since it was built, any change in~$x$ would naturally cause no change whatever in~$y$; in this case $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ has no meaning whatever, and it is not possible to find an expression for it.
excerpts.markdown: If, while $x$ is, as before, the distance of the foot of the ladder from the wall, $y$ is, instead of the height reached, the horizontal length of the wall, or the number of bricks in it, or the number of years since it was built, any change in $x$ would naturally cause no change whatever in $y$; in this case $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ has no meaning whatever, and it is not possible to find an expression for it.
excerpts.why: Warns that dy/dx only means something when y really depends on x, using a counter-example the learner can picture.

excerpts.latex: It will never do to fall into the schoolboy error of thinking that $dx$ means $d$~times~$x$, for $d$ is not a factor---it means ``an element of'' or ``a bit of'' whatever follows.
excerpts.markdown: It will never do to fall into the schoolboy error of thinking that $dx$ means $d$ times $x$, for $d$ is not a factor---it means “an element of” or “a bit of” whatever follows.
excerpts.why: Heads off the common mistake of reading dx as a product.

excerpts.latex: Now remember that the fundamental notion about the calculus is the idea of \emph{growing}. Mathematicians call it \emph{varying}.
excerpts.markdown: Now remember that the fundamental notion about the calculus is the idea of *growing*. Mathematicians call it *varying*.
excerpts.why: Gives the learner the central intuition of the calculus, growing, before any symbols are used.

excerpts.latex: Then $(dx)^2$~will mean a little bit of a little bit of~$x$; that is, as explained above (\Pageref{smallness}), it is a small quantity of the second order of smallness. It may therefore be discarded as quite inconsiderable in comparison with the other terms.
excerpts.markdown: Then $(dx)^2$ will mean a little bit of a little bit of $x$; that is, as explained above (smallness), it is a small quantity of the second order of smallness. It may therefore be discarded as quite inconsiderable in comparison with the other terms.
excerpts.why: Explains in plain words why the (dx)^2 term can be dropped in the working.

excerpts.latex: But, you will say, we neglected a whole unit.
excerpts.markdown: But, you will say, we neglected a whole unit.
excerpts.why: Voices the learner's natural objection to discarding a term, which the next step answers by making dx smaller.

excerpts.latex: Just look at these results: the operation of differentiating appears to have had the effect of diminishing the power of~$x$ by~$1$ (for example in the last case reducing $x^4$ to~$x^3$), and at the same time multiplying by a number (the same number in fact which originally appeared as the power).
excerpts.markdown: Just look at these results: the operation of differentiating appears to have had the effect of diminishing the power of $x$ by $1$ (for example in the last case reducing $x^4$ to $x^3$), and at the same time multiplying by a number (the same number in fact which originally appeared as the power).
excerpts.why: Shows how a general rule is guessed from a pattern in worked cases.

excerpts.latex: To differentiate~$x^n$, multiply by the power and reduce the power by one, so giving us~$nx^{n-1}$ as the result.
excerpts.markdown: To differentiate $x^n$, multiply by the power and reduce the power by one, so giving us $nx^{n-1}$ as the result.
excerpts.why: States the power rule as a short procedure a learner can follow.

excerpts.latex: You have now learned how to differentiate powers of~$x$. How easy it is!
excerpts.markdown: You have now learned how to differentiate powers of $x$. How easy it is!
excerpts.why: Ends the chapter with the book's encouraging tone.

excerpts.latex: Now we know that we may neglect small quantities of the second and third orders; since, when $dy$~and~$dx$ are both made indefinitely small, $(dx)^2$~and~$(dx)^3$ will become indefinitely smaller by comparison.
excerpts.markdown: Now we know that we may neglect small quantities of the second and third orders; since, when $dy$ and $dx$ are both made indefinitely small, $(dx)^2$ and $(dx)^3$ will become indefinitely smaller by comparison.
excerpts.why: It gives the reason why second- and higher-order terms in dx can be dropped, which is the step learners most often question.

excerpts.latex: But, you will say, we neglected a whole unit. Well, try again, making $dx$ a still smaller bit.
excerpts.markdown: But, you will say, we neglected a whole unit. Well, try again, making $dx$ a still smaller bit.
excerpts.why: It anticipates a learner's objection to the numerical check and shows how a smaller dx settles it.

excerpts.location: Next Stage. What to do with Constants
excerpts.latex: So if we take the letter~$a$, or~$b$, or~$c$ to represent any constant, it will simply disappear when we differentiate.
excerpts.markdown: So if we take the letter $a$, or $b$, or $c$ to represent any constant, it will simply disappear when we differentiate.
excerpts.why: It generalises the vanishing of a constant to any symbol standing for a constant.

excerpts.location: Next Stage. What to do with Constants
excerpts.latex: If we had begun with $y = ax^n$, we should have had $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = a×nx^{n-1}$.
excerpts.markdown: If we had begun with $y = ax^n$, we should have had $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = a×nx^{n-1}$.
excerpts.why: It gives the general power rule with a constant coefficient in a single line a learner can test against examples.

excerpts.location: Next Stage. What to do with Constants
excerpts.latex: And, what is true about multiplication is equally true about \emph{division}: for if, in the example above, we had taken as the constant~$\frac{1}{7}$ instead of~$7$, we should have had the same~$\frac{1}{7}$ come out in the result after differentiation.
excerpts.markdown: And, what is true about multiplication is equally true about *division*: for if, in the example above, we had taken as the constant $\frac{1}{7}$ instead of $7$, we should have had the same $\frac{1}{7}$ come out in the result after differentiation.
excerpts.why: It extends the constant-factor rule to division, so a learner sees that a fractional constant behaves the same way.

excerpts.location: Next Stage. What to do with Constants
excerpts.latex: We usually think of $x$ as a quantity that we can vary; and, regarding the variation of~$x$ as a sort of \emph{cause}, we consider the resulting variation of~$y$ as an \emph{effect}. In other words, we regard the value of~$y$ as depending on that of~$x$.
excerpts.markdown: We usually think of $x$ as a quantity that we can vary; and, regarding the variation of $x$ as a sort of *cause*, we consider the resulting variation of $y$ as an *effect*. In other words, we regard the value of $y$ as depending on that of $x$.
excerpts.why: Gives the learner a cause-and-effect picture of the independent and dependent variable.

excerpts.location: Next Stage. What to do with Constants
excerpts.latex: So the $5$ has quite disappeared. It added nothing to the growth of~$x$, and does not enter into the differential coefficient.
excerpts.markdown: So the $5$ has quite disappeared. It added nothing to the growth of $x$, and does not enter into the differential coefficient.
excerpts.why: Explains in plain words why an added constant drops out of the derivative.

excerpts.location: Next Stage. What to do with Constants
excerpts.latex: So that any mere multiplication by a constant reappears as a mere multiplication when the thing is differentiated. And, what is true about multiplication is equally true about \emph{division}: for if, in the example above, we had taken as the constant~$\frac{1}{7}$ instead of~$7$, we should have had the same~$\frac{1}{7}$ come out in the result after differentiation.
excerpts.markdown: So that any mere multiplication by a constant reappears as a mere multiplication when the thing is differentiated. And, what is true about multiplication is equally true about *division*: for if, in the example above, we had taken as the constant $\frac{1}{7}$ instead of $7$, we should have had the same $\frac{1}{7}$ come out in the result after differentiation.
excerpts.why: States the constant-multiple rule and extends it to division, in contrast with the added-constant case.

excerpts.location: Next Stage. What to do with Constants
excerpts.latex: As a rule an expression of this kind will need a little more knowledge than we have acquired so far; it is, however, always worth while to try whether the expression can be put in a simpler form.
excerpts.markdown: As a rule an expression of this kind will need a little more knowledge than we have acquired so far; it is, however, always worth while to try whether the expression can be put in a simpler form.
excerpts.why: Teaches the habit of trying to simplify an awkward expression before differentiating.

excerpts.location: Next Stage. What to do with Constants
excerpts.latex: If $r = 5.5$~in.\ and $h=20$~in.\ this becomes $690.8$. It means that a change of radius of $1$~inch will cause a change of volume of $690.8$~cub.~inch. This can be easily verified, for the volumes with $r = 5$~and $r = 6$ are $1570$~cub.~in.\ and $2260.8$~cub.~in.\ respectively, and $2260.8 - 1570 = 690.8$.
excerpts.markdown: If $r = 5.5$ in. and $h=20$ in. this becomes $690.8$. It means that a change of radius of $1$ inch will cause a change of volume of $690.8$ cub. inch. This can be easily verified, for the volumes with $r = 5$ and $r = 6$ are $1570$ cub. in. and $2260.8$ cub. in. respectively, and $2260.8 - 1570 = 690.8$.
excerpts.why: Shows how to interpret a derivative as a rate and check it against direct subtraction.

excerpts.location: Next Stage. What to do with Constants
excerpts.latex: The sensitiveness is approximately doubled from $800°$~to $1000°$, and becomes three-quarters as great again up to~$1200°$.
excerpts.markdown: The sensitiveness is approximately doubled from $800°$ to $1000°$, and becomes three-quarters as great again up to $1200°$.
excerpts.why: Shows how to read a derivative's values in a physical setting, here the sensitivity of a pyrometer.

excerpts.latex: If you have any doubt whether this is right, try a more general case, working it by first principles. And this is the way.
excerpts.markdown: If you have any doubt whether this is right, try a more general case, working it by first principles. And this is the way.
excerpts.why: It encourages the learner to check a rule by deriving it from first principles rather than trusting memory.

excerpts.latex: This justifies the procedure. You differentiate each function separately and add the results.
excerpts.markdown: This justifies the procedure. You differentiate each function separately and add the results.
excerpts.why: States the sum rule plainly right after its first-principles proof.

excerpts.latex: The result will certainly \emph{not} be $2x × 4ax^3$; for it is easy to see that neither $c × ax^4$, nor $x^2 × b$, would have been taken into that product.
excerpts.markdown: The result will certainly *not* be $2x × 4ax^3$; for it is easy to see that neither $c × ax^4$, nor $x^2 × b$, would have been taken into that product.
excerpts.why: Warns against the tempting mistake of multiplying the separate derivatives.

excerpts.latex: \emph{To differentiate the product of two functions, multiply each function by the differential coefficient of the other, and add together the two products so obtained.}
excerpts.markdown: *To differentiate the product of two functions, multiply each function by the differential coefficient of the other, and add together the two products so obtained.*
excerpts.why: The product rule in one clear sentence of instruction.

excerpts.latex: You should note that this process amounts to the following: Treat~$u$ as constant while you differentiate~$v$; then treat~$v$ as constant while you differentiate~$u$; and the whole differential coefficient~$\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ will be the sum of these two treatments.
excerpts.markdown: You should note that this process amounts to the following: Treat $u$ as constant while you differentiate $v$; then treat $v$ as constant while you differentiate $u$; and the whole differential coefficient $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ will be the sum of these two treatments.
excerpts.why: Gives a memorable way to think about the product rule.

excerpts.latex: This gives us our instructions as to \textit{how to differentiate a quotient \emph{of two functions}. Multiply the divisor function by the differential coefficient of the dividend function; then multiply the dividend function by the differential coefficient of the divisor function; and subtract. Lastly divide by the square of the divisor function}.
excerpts.markdown: This gives us our instructions as to *how to differentiate a quotient *of two functions*. Multiply the divisor function by the differential coefficient of the dividend function; then multiply the dividend function by the differential coefficient of the divisor function; and subtract. Lastly divide by the square of the divisor function*.
excerpts.why: States the quotient rule as a step-by-step procedure in words.

excerpts.latex: The working out of quotients is often tedious, but there is nothing difficult about it.
excerpts.markdown: The working out of quotients is often tedious, but there is nothing difficult about it.
excerpts.why: Reassures learners that the quotient rule is laborious but not hard.

excerpts.latex: Now $du · dv$ is a small quantity of the second order of smallness, and therefore in the limit may be discarded, leaving
excerpts.markdown: Now $du · dv$ is a small quantity of the second order of smallness, and therefore in the limit may be discarded, leaving
excerpts.why: Shows why the du·dv term drops out of the product-rule derivation.

excerpts.latex: In such a case it is no use to try to work out the division beforehand, because $x^2 + a$ will not divide into $bx^5 + c$, neither have they any common factor.
excerpts.markdown: In such a case it is no use to try to work out the division beforehand, because $x^2 + a$ will not divide into $bx^5 + c$, neither have they any common factor.
excerpts.why: Explains when the quotient rule is needed rather than simplifying first.

excerpts.latex: Begin with a concrete case.
excerpts.markdown: Begin with a concrete case.
excerpts.why: It tells the learner to start from a specific power before the general case, which is a sound teaching order.

excerpts.latex: This is called the ``derived function'' of~$x$.
excerpts.markdown: This is called the “derived function” of $x$.
excerpts.why: It names the derivative of a function, so the learner knows what the new function is called.

excerpts.latex:
So the
statement $y=f(x)$ merely tells us that $y$ is a function
of~$x$, it may be $x^2$ or $ax^n$, or $\cos x$ or any other complicated
function of~$x$.
excerpts.markdown: So the statement $y=f(x)$ merely tells us that $y$ is a function of $x$, it may be $x^2$ or $ax^n$, or $\cos x$ or any other complicated function of $x$.
excerpts.why: It makes the general symbol f(x) concrete by listing several functions it could stand for.

excerpts.latex: This is to employ the general symbol~$f(x)$ for any function of~$x$. Here the symbol~$f(~)$ is read as ``function of,'' without saying what particular function is meant. So the statement $y=f(x)$ merely tells us that $y$ is a function of~$x$, it may be $x^2$ or $ax^n$, or $\cos x$ or any other complicated function of~$x$.
excerpts.markdown: This is to employ the general symbol $f(x)$ for any function of $x$. Here the symbol $f(~)$ is read as “function of,” without saying what particular function is meant. So the statement $y=f(x)$ merely tells us that $y$ is a function of $x$, it may be $x^2$ or $ax^n$, or $\cos x$ or any other complicated function of $x$.
excerpts.why: Explains plainly what f(x) means: a placeholder for any function, not one particular formula.

excerpts.latex: The corresponding symbol for the differential coefficient is~$f'(x)$, which is simpler to write than $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$. This is called the ``derived function'' of~$x$.
excerpts.markdown: The corresponding symbol for the differential coefficient is $f'(x)$, which is simpler to write than $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$. This is called the “derived function” of $x$.
excerpts.why: Introduces the primed notation for the derivative and the older name 'derived function'.

excerpts.latex: Suppose we differentiate over again, we shall get the ``second derived function'' or second differential coefficient, which is denoted by~$f''(x)$; and so on.
excerpts.markdown: Suppose we differentiate over again, we shall get the “second derived function” or second differential coefficient, which is denoted by $f''(x)$; and so on.
excerpts.why: Shows in one sentence that differentiating again gives the next derivative, with its notation.

excerpts.latex: Similarly, we may write as the result of thrice differentiating, $\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3} = f'''(x)$.
excerpts.markdown: Similarly, we may write as the result of thrice differentiating, $\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3} = f'''(x)$.
excerpts.why: Links the d^3y/dx^3 notation to the primed notation so learners can read both.

excerpts.latex: What do we mean by \emph{rate}? In both these cases we are making a mental comparison of something that is happening, and the length of time that it takes to happen.
excerpts.markdown: What do we mean by *rate*? In both these cases we are making a mental comparison of something that is happening, and the length of time that it takes to happen.
excerpts.why: It gives learners a plain everyday meaning of rate as a comparison between what happens and the time it takes, before any calculus.

excerpts.latex: Ten yards is not the same as $600$~yards, nor is one second the same thing as one minute. What we mean by saying that the \emph{rate} is the same, is this: that the proportion borne between distance passed over and time taken to pass over it, is the same in both cases.
excerpts.markdown: Ten yards is not the same as $600$ yards, nor is one second the same thing as one minute. What we mean by saying that the *rate* is the same, is this: that the proportion borne between distance passed over and time taken to pass over it, is the same in both cases.
excerpts.why: It shows that two different speeds can share one rate because the ratio of distance to time is what matters.

excerpts.latex: He did not use the notation of the $dy$ and~$dx$, and~$dt$ (this was due to Leibnitz), but had instead a notation of his own.
excerpts.markdown: He did not use the notation of the $dy$ and $dx$, and $dt$ (this was due to Leibnitz), but had instead a notation of his own.
excerpts.why: It places the dot notation historically, so learners understand why two notations for the same rate exist.

excerpts.latex: The force necessary to accelerate a mass is proportional to the mass, and it is also proportional to the acceleration which is being imparted.
excerpts.markdown: The force necessary to accelerate a mass is proportional to the mass, and it is also proportional to the acceleration which is being imparted.
excerpts.why: It gives the reasoning behind f = ma in plain words before the symbols are written.

excerpts.latex: Again, if a force is employed to move something (against an equal and opposite counter-force), it does \emph{work}; and the amount of work done is measured by the product of the force into the distance (in its own direction) through which its point of application moves forward.
excerpts.markdown: Again, if a force is employed to move something (against an equal and opposite counter-force), it does *work*; and the amount of work done is measured by the product of the force into the distance (in its own direction) through which its point of application moves forward.
excerpts.why: It defines work as force times displacement in the force's own direction, a definition learners can check by example.

excerpts.latex: When a railway train has just begun to move, its velocity~$v$ is small; but it is rapidly gaining speed---it is being hurried up, or accelerated, by the effort of the engine. So its $\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2}$ is large. When it has got up its top speed it is no longer being accelerated, so that then $\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2}$ has fallen to zero.
excerpts.markdown: When a railway train has just begun to move, its velocity $v$ is small; but it is rapidly gaining speed---it is being hurried up, or accelerated, by the effort of the engine. So its $\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2}$ is large. When it has got up its top speed it is no longer being accelerated, so that then $\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2}$ has fallen to zero.
excerpts.why: Gives a physical picture of what the second derivative is doing as a train starts and then cruises.

excerpts.latex: But this notation does not tell us what is the independent variable with respect to which the differentiation has been effected. When we see $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$ we know that $y$ is to be differentiated with respect to~$t$.
excerpts.markdown: But this notation does not tell us what is the independent variable with respect to which the differentiation has been effected. When we see $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$ we know that $y$ is to be differentiated with respect to $t$.
excerpts.why: Shows the strength of Leibniz's notation over Newton's dots, which hide the variable of differentiation.

excerpts.latex: What we mean by saying that the \emph{rate} is the same, is this: that the proportion borne between distance passed over and time taken to pass over it, is the same in both cases.
excerpts.markdown: What we mean by saying that the *rate* is the same, is this: that the proportion borne between distance passed over and time taken to pass over it, is the same in both cases.
excerpts.why: Explains why 10 yards per second and 600 yards per minute count as the same rate, even though neither the distances nor the times are equal.

excerpts.latex: It is said that Sandy had not been in London above five minutes when ``bang went saxpence.''
excerpts.markdown: It is said that Sandy had not been in London above five minutes when “bang went saxpence.”
excerpts.why: A humorous anecdote that makes the idea of spending money at a rate memorable.

excerpts.latex: Now the speed was not actually constant all the way: at starting, and during the slowing up at the end of the journey, the speed was less. Probably at some part, when running downhill, the speed was over $60$~miles an hour. If, during any particular element of time~$dt$, the corresponding element of distance passed over was~$dy$, then at that part of the journey the speed was~$\dfrac{dy}{dt}$.
excerpts.markdown: Now the speed was not actually constant all the way: at starting, and during the slowing up at the end of the journey, the speed was less. Probably at some part, when running downhill, the speed was over $60$ miles an hour. If, during any particular element of time $dt$, the corresponding element of distance passed over was $dy$, then at that part of the journey the speed was $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$.
excerpts.why: Contrasts a journey's average speed with its speed at an instant, which leads into dy/dt.

excerpts.latex: That is to say, force may be expressed either as mass times acceleration, or as rate of change of momentum.
excerpts.markdown: That is to say, force may be expressed either as mass times acceleration, or as rate of change of momentum.
excerpts.why: States the two equivalent forms of force that the preceding derivation arrives at.

excerpts.latex: In this last sentence the word \emph{rate} is clearly not used in its time-sense, but in its meaning as ratio or proportion.
excerpts.markdown: In this last sentence the word *rate* is clearly not used in its time-sense, but in its meaning as ratio or proportion.
excerpts.why: Warns that rate does not always mean change per unit time, as in work done per unit of length.

excerpts.latex: (It is the same velocity as the velocity at the middle of the interval, $t = 5$; for, the acceleration being constant, the velocity has varied uniformly from zero when $t = 0$ to $4~\text{ft./sec.}$ when $t = 10$.)
excerpts.markdown: (It is the same velocity as the velocity at the middle of the interval, $t = 5$; for, the acceleration being constant, the velocity has varied uniformly from zero when $t = 0$ to $4~\text{ft./sec.}$ when $t = 10$.)
excerpts.why: Explains why average velocity equals the midpoint velocity when acceleration is constant, a point the later examples show failing when it is not.

excerpts.latex: Thus, the equation\Pagelabel{dodge} \[ y = (x^2+a^2)^{\efrac{3}{2}} \] is awkward to a beginner.
excerpts.markdown: Thus, the equationdodge $$y = (x^2+a^2)^{\efrac{3}{2}}$$ is awkward to a beginner.
excerpts.why: It gives the concrete example that the rest of the chapter works through.

excerpts.latex:
\First{Sometimes} one is stumped by finding that the expression
to be differentiated is too complicated to
tackle directly.
excerpts.markdown: Sometimes one is stumped by finding that the expression to be differentiated is too complicated to tackle directly.
excerpts.why: It names the problem the chapter solves: an expression that looks too tangled to differentiate in one step.

excerpts.latex:
By and bye,\DPnote{** TN: [sic], archaic spelling} when you have learned how to deal
with sines, and cosines, and exponentials, you will
find this dodge of increasing usefulness.
excerpts.markdown: By and bye, when you have learned how to deal with sines, and cosines, and exponentials, you will find this dodge of increasing usefulness.
excerpts.why: It tells the learner the dodge is a tool they will keep using later, in a charming old voice.

excerpts.latex:
The process can be extended to three or more
differential coefficients, so that $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy}{dz} × \dfrac{dz}{dv} × \dfrac{dv}{dx}$.
excerpts.markdown: The process can be extended to three or more differential coefficients, so that $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy}{dz} × \dfrac{dz}{dv} × \dfrac{dv}{dx}$.
excerpts.why: It shows the dodge can be chained through several intermediate variables.

excerpts.latex:
(We may also write $y = (1-x)^{\efrac{1}{2}} (1+x)^{-\efrac{1}{2}}$ and differentiate
as a product.)
excerpts.markdown: (We may also write $y = (1-x)^{\efrac{1}{2}} (1+x)^{-\efrac{1}{2}}$ and differentiate as a product.)
excerpts.why: It reminds the learner that one function can be differentiated by more than one route.

excerpts.latex:
(1) Differentiate $y = \sqrt{a+x}$.

Let $a+x = u$.
excerpts.markdown: (1) Differentiate $y = \sqrt{a+x}$. Let $a+x = u$.
excerpts.why: It is the simplest worked case of the dodge: name the inner expression u, then proceed.

excerpts.latex: This tangent to the curve has evidently the same slope as~$QT$, so that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point~$Q$ for which the value of~$\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is found.
excerpts.markdown: This tangent to the curve has evidently the same slope as $QT$, so that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $Q$ for which the value of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is found.
excerpts.why: It links the derivative directly to the tangent's slope, the central geometric idea of the chapter.

excerpts.latex: For a horizontal line, or a horizontal place in a curve, $dy=0$, and therefore~$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
excerpts.markdown: For a horizontal line, or a horizontal place in a curve, $dy=0$, and therefore $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
excerpts.why: It tells a learner that a zero derivative means a horizontal tangent.

excerpts.latex: We have seen that the short expression ``the slope of a curve'' has no precise meaning, because a curve has so many slopes---in fact, every small portion of a curve has a different slope.
excerpts.markdown: We have seen that the short expression “the slope of a curve” has no precise meaning, because a curve has so many slopes---in fact, every small portion of a curve has a different slope.
excerpts.why: Warns learners that 'the slope of a curve' is ill-defined until a point is named.

excerpts.latex: ``The slope of a curve \emph{at a point}'' is, however, a perfectly defined thing; it is the slope of a very small portion of the curve situated just at that point; and we have seen that this is the same as ``the slope of the tangent to the curve at that point.''
excerpts.markdown: “The slope of a curve *at a point*” is, however, a perfectly defined thing; it is the slope of a very small portion of the curve situated just at that point; and we have seen that this is the same as “the slope of the tangent to the curve at that point.”
excerpts.why: Gives the precise meaning of slope at a point and ties it to the tangent.

excerpts.latex: Observe that $dx$ is a short step to the right, and $dy$ the corresponding short step upwards. These steps must be considered as short as possible---in fact indefinitely short,---though in diagrams we have to represent them by bits that are not infinitesimally small, otherwise they could not be seen.
excerpts.markdown: Observe that $dx$ is a short step to the right, and $dy$ the corresponding short step upwards. These steps must be considered as short as possible---in fact indefinitely short,---though in diagrams we have to represent them by bits that are not infinitesimally small, otherwise they could not be seen.
excerpts.why: Explains honestly why diagrams exaggerate the tiny steps dx and dy.

excerpts.latex: If a curve is sloping up at~$45°$ at a particular point, as in \Fig{8}, $dy$ and~$dx$ will be equal, and the value of $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1$.
excerpts.markdown: If a curve is sloping up at $45°$ at a particular point, as in [fig:8]Fig. 8, $dy$ and $dx$ will be equal, and the value of $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1$.
excerpts.why: Gives a concrete benchmark for reading slope values from a picture.

excerpts.latex: If a curve slopes \emph{downward}, as in \Fig{11}, $dy$~will be a step down, and must therefore be reckoned of negative value; hence $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$~will have negative sign also.
excerpts.markdown: If a curve slopes *downward*, as in [fig:11]Fig. 11, $dy$ will be a step down, and must therefore be reckoned of negative value; hence $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ will have negative sign also.
excerpts.why: Shows why a descending curve has a negative slope.

excerpts.latex: The characteristic of a minimum is that $y$~must increase \emph{on either side} of it.
excerpts.markdown: The characteristic of a minimum is that $y$ must increase *on either side* of it.
excerpts.why: Corrects the common idea that a minimum is simply the smallest value.

excerpts.latex: The slope of the tangent is the slope of the curve at the point where they touch one another (see \Pageref{slope}); that is, it is the $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ of the curve for that point.
excerpts.markdown: The slope of the tangent is the slope of the curve at the point where they touch one another (see slope); that is, it is the $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ of the curve for that point.
excerpts.why: Starts the worked method for finding a tangent: use dy/dx at the touching point.

excerpts.latex: In all exercises dealing with curves, students will find it extremely instructive to verify the deductions obtained by actually plotting the curves.
excerpts.markdown: In all exercises dealing with curves, students will find it extremely instructive to verify the deductions obtained by actually plotting the curves.
excerpts.why: Encourages checking calculations against a drawn curve.

excerpts.latex: So, writing $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$ does \emph{not} mean that it always is $=0$; but you write it down \emph{as a condition} in order to see how much $x$ will come out if $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is to be zero.
excerpts.markdown: So, writing $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$ does *not* mean that it always is $=0$; but you write it down *as a condition* in order to see how much $x$ will come out if $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is to be zero.
excerpts.why: It explains that the equation dy/dx = 0 is an equation of condition, true only at the particular point sought.

excerpts.latex: It does not of itself discriminate; it finds for you the right value of~$x$ but leaves you to find out for yourselves whether the corresponding~$y$ is a maximum or a minimum.
excerpts.markdown: It does not of itself discriminate; it finds for you the right value of $x$ but leaves you to find out for yourselves whether the corresponding $y$ is a maximum or a minimum.
excerpts.why: It warns the learner that setting the derivative to zero finds the candidate point but does not say whether it is a maximum or a minimum.

excerpts.latex: It is necessary therefore always to check by taking one value on either side.
excerpts.markdown: It is necessary therefore always to check by taking one value on either side.
excerpts.why: It gives the learner the habit of checking a stationary point on both sides before calling it a maximum or minimum.

excerpts.latex: Let the number to be cut into two parts be called~$n$. Then if $x$ is one part, the other will be~$n-x$, and the product will be $x(n-x)$ or~$nx-x^2$. So we write $y=nx-x^2$.
excerpts.markdown: Let the number to be cut into two parts be called $n$. Then if $x$ is one part, the other will be $n-x$, and the product will be $x(n-x)$ or $nx-x^2$. So we write $y=nx-x^2$.
excerpts.why: It shows how a word problem is turned into a function of one variable before differentiating.

excerpts.latex: This is a very useful rule, and applies to any number of factors, so that if $m+n+p=$ a constant number, $m×n×p$ is a maximum when $m=n=p$.
excerpts.markdown: This is a very useful rule, and applies to any number of factors, so that if $m+n+p=$ a constant number, $m×n×p$ is a maximum when $m=n=p$.
excerpts.why: It states a general result the learner can apply: a fixed sum of factors has its largest product when the factors are equal.

excerpts.latex: \First{One} of the principal uses of the process of differentiating is to find out under what conditions the value of the thing differentiated becomes a maximum, or a minimum. This is often exceedingly important in engineering questions, where it is most desirable to know what conditions will make the cost of working a minimum, or will make the efficiency a maximum.
excerpts.markdown: One of the principal uses of the process of differentiating is to find out under what conditions the value of the thing differentiated becomes a maximum, or a minimum. This is often exceedingly important in engineering questions, where it is most desirable to know what conditions will make the cost of working a minimum, or will make the efficiency a maximum.
excerpts.why: States why maxima and minima matter in practice, giving learners a reason to care.

excerpts.latex: Now it may sound like juggling to be assured that there is a way by which one can arrive straight at a maximum (or minimum) value without making a lot of preliminary trials or guesses.
excerpts.markdown: Now it may sound like juggling to be assured that there is a way by which one can arrive straight at a maximum (or minimum) value without making a lot of preliminary trials or guesses.
excerpts.why: Voices the learner's natural suspicion before the method is introduced.

excerpts.latex: When there is put before you an equation, and you want to find that value of~$x$ that will make its~$y$ a minimum (or a maximum), \emph{first differentiate it}, and having done so, write its $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ as \emph{equal to zero}, and then solve for~$x$. Put this particular value of~$x$ into the original equation, and you will then get the required value of~$y$. This process is commonly called ``equating to zero.''
excerpts.markdown: When there is put before you an equation, and you want to find that value of $x$ that will make its $y$ a minimum (or a maximum), *first differentiate it*, and having done so, write its $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ as *equal to zero*, and then solve for $x$. Put this particular value of $x$ into the original equation, and you will then get the required value of $y$. This process is commonly called “equating to zero.”
excerpts.why: Gives the whole method in one passage, in order.

excerpts.latex: Ordinarily you are dealing with equations that are true in themselves, but, on occasions, of which the present are examples, you have to write down equations that are not necessarily true, but are only true if certain conditions are to be fulfilled; and you write them down in order, by solving them, to find the conditions which make them true.
excerpts.markdown: Ordinarily you are dealing with equations that are true in themselves, but, on occasions, of which the present are examples, you have to write down equations that are not necessarily true, but are only true if certain conditions are to be fulfilled; and you write them down in order, by solving them, to find the conditions which make them true.
excerpts.why: Explains why writing dy/dx = 0 is a condition we impose and not a claim that the slope is always zero.

excerpts.latex: Quite so. It does not of itself discriminate; it finds for you the right value of~$x$ but leaves you to find out for yourselves whether the corresponding~$y$ is a maximum or a minimum. Of course, if you have plotted the curve, you know already which it will be.
excerpts.markdown: Quite so. It does not of itself discriminate; it finds for you the right value of $x$ but leaves you to find out for yourselves whether the corresponding $y$ is a maximum or a minimum. Of course, if you have plotted the curve, you know already which it will be.
excerpts.why: Warns that setting the derivative to zero finds the turning point but does not say which kind it is.

excerpts.latex: So now we \emph{know} that whatever number $n$ may be, we must divide it into two equal parts if the product of the parts is to be a maximum; and the value of that maximum product will always be $ = \tfrac{1}{4} n^2$.
excerpts.markdown: So now we *know* that whatever number $n$ may be, we must divide it into two equal parts if the product of the parts is to be a maximum; and the value of that maximum product will always be $ = \tfrac{1}{4} n^2$.
excerpts.why: Shows the calculus giving a general result that the trial-and-error table only hinted at for 60.

excerpts.latex: On plotting the graph it will be found that the curve goes to the origin, as if there were a minimum there; but instead of continuing beyond, as it should do for a minimum, it retraces its steps (forming what is called a ``cusp''). There is no minimum, therefore, although the condition for a minimum is satisfied, namely $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$. It is necessary therefore always to check by taking one value on either side.
excerpts.markdown: On plotting the graph it will be found that the curve goes to the origin, as if there were a minimum there; but instead of continuing beyond, as it should do for a minimum, it retraces its steps (forming what is called a “cusp”). There is no minimum, therefore, although the condition for a minimum is satisfied, namely $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$. It is necessary therefore always to check by taking one value on either side.
excerpts.why: Warns that dy/dx = 0 can hold where there is no minimum, so the answer must be checked.

excerpts.latex: Clearly it means the rate (per unit of length~$x$) at which the slope is changing---in brief, it is \emph{a measure of the curvature of the slope}.
excerpts.markdown: Clearly it means the rate (per unit of length $x$) at which the slope is changing---in brief, it is *a measure of the curvature of the slope*.
excerpts.why: It gives the learner a physical picture of the second derivative as the rate at which the slope itself changes.

excerpts.latex: If $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ comes out \emph{positive}, then you know that the value of~$y$ which you got was a \emph{minimum}; but if $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ comes out \emph{negative}, then the value of~$y$ which you got must be a \emph{maximum}. That's the rule.
excerpts.markdown: If $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ comes out *positive*, then you know that the value of $y$ which you got was a *minimum*; but if $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ comes out *negative*, then the value of $y$ which you got must be a *maximum*. That’s the rule.
excerpts.why: It states the second derivative test compactly so the learner can apply it to any stationary value.

excerpts.latex: To the left of~$M$ the slope is downward, that is, negative, and is getting less negative.
excerpts.markdown: To the left of $M$ the slope is downward, that is, negative, and is getting less negative.
excerpts.why: It explains in plain terms why a positive second derivative goes with a minimum, by tracking the sign of the slope.

excerpts.latex: But what can $\dfrac{d^2 y}{dx^2}$~mean in this case? Clearly it means the rate (per unit of length~$x$) at which the slope is changing---in brief, it is \emph{a measure of the curvature of the slope}.
excerpts.markdown: But what can $\dfrac{d^2 y}{dx^2}$ mean in this case? Clearly it means the rate (per unit of length $x$) at which the slope is changing---in brief, it is *a measure of the curvature of the slope*.
excerpts.why: Answers the learner's question of why anyone differentiates twice, by giving the second derivative a plain geometric meaning.

excerpts.latex: It is now time to initiate you into another secret---how to tell whether the result that you get by ``equating to zero'' is a maximum or a minimum. The trick is this: After you have differentiated (so as to get the expression which you equate to zero), you then differentiate a second time, and look whether the result of the second differentiation is \emph{positive} or \emph{negative}. If $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ comes out \emph{positive}, then you know that the value of~$y$ which you got was a \emph{minimum}; but if $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ comes out \emph{negative}, then the value of~$y$ which you got must be a \emph{maximum}. That's the rule.
excerpts.markdown: It is now time to initiate you into another secret---how to tell whether the result that you get by “equating to zero” is a maximum or a minimum. The trick is this: After you have differentiated (so as to get the expression which you equate to zero), you then differentiate a second time, and look whether the result of the second differentiation is *positive* or *negative*. If $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ comes out *positive*, then you know that the value of $y$ which you got was a *minimum*; but if $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ comes out *negative*, then the value of $y$ which you got must be a *maximum*. That’s the rule.
excerpts.why: States the second-derivative test as a short, memorable procedure.

excerpts.latex: Clearly the change of slope as the curve passes through~$M$ is such that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$~is \emph{positive}, for its operation, as $x$~increases toward the right, is to convert a downward slope into an upward one.
excerpts.markdown: Clearly the change of slope as the curve passes through $M$ is such that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ is *positive*, for its operation, as $x$ increases toward the right, is to convert a downward slope into an upward one.
excerpts.why: Explains why a minimum goes with a positive second derivative, using the picture of the slope turning from downward to upward.

excerpts.latex: In this case, as the curve passes through~$M$ from left to right, its upward slope is converted into a downward or negative slope, so that in this case the ``slope of the slope'' $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ is \emph{negative}.
excerpts.markdown: In this case, as the curve passes through $M$ from left to right, its upward slope is converted into a downward or negative slope, so that in this case the “slope of the slope” $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ is *negative*.
excerpts.why: Gives the matching picture for a maximum, with the slope turning from upward to downward.

excerpts.latex: The denominator is always positive, so it is sufficient to ascertain the sign of the numerator.
excerpts.markdown: The denominator is always positive, so it is sufficient to ascertain the sign of the numerator.
excerpts.why: Shows a practical shortcut: when testing the sign of a messy second derivative, only the sign of the numerator matters.

excerpts.latex: The expense~$C$ of handling the products of a certain factory varies with the weekly output~$P$ according to the relation $C = aP + \dfrac{b}{c+P} + d$, where $a$,~$b$, $c$,~$d$ are positive constants. For what output will the expense be least?
excerpts.markdown: The expense $C$ of handling the products of a certain factory varies with the weekly output $P$ according to the relation $C = aP + \dfrac{b}{c+P} + d$, where $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ are positive constants. For what output will the expense be least?
excerpts.why: Poses a real-world minimising problem that the chapter's method then solves.

excerpts.latex: If we perform many additions of two or more fractions the denominators of which contain only terms in~$x$, and no terms in $x^2$,~$x^3$, or any other powers of~$x$, we \emph{always} find that \emph{the denominator of the final resulting fraction is the product of the denominators} of the fractions which were added to form the result.
excerpts.markdown: If we perform many additions of two or more fractions the denominators of which contain only terms in $x$, and no terms in $x^2$, $x^3$, or any other powers of $x$, we *always* find that *the denominator of the final resulting fraction is the product of the denominators* of the fractions which were added to form the result.
excerpts.why: It states the rule that tells a learner how to recover the denominators of the partial fractions by factoring the final denominator.

excerpts.latex: If we make $x=1$, we get $4 = (A × 0)+(B × 2)$, so that $B=2$; and if we make $x=-1$, we get $-2 = (A × -2) + (B × 0)$, so that $A=1$.
excerpts.markdown: If we make $x=1$, we get $4 = (A × 0)+(B × 2)$, so that $B=2$; and if we make $x=-1$, we get $-2 = (A × -2) + (B × 0)$, so that $A=1$.
excerpts.why: It shows a worked step in which substituting convenient values of x isolates each unknown numerator.

excerpts.latex: Since the given fraction and the fraction found by adding the partial fractions are equal, and have \emph{identical} denominators, the numerators must also be identically the same. In such a case, and for such algebraical expressions as those with which we are dealing here, \emph{the coefficients of the same powers of~$x$ are equal and of same sign}.
excerpts.markdown: Since the given fraction and the fraction found by adding the partial fractions are equal, and have *identical* denominators, the numerators must also be identically the same. In such a case, and for such algebraical expressions as those with which we are dealing here, *the coefficients of the same powers of $x$ are equal and of same sign*.
excerpts.why: It explains why equal polynomials give equations between their coefficients, which a learner needs before solving for the unknown numerators.

excerpts.latex: If we could split the fraction into two or more simpler fractions such that their sum is equivalent to the original fraction, we could then proceed by differentiating each of these simpler expressions.
excerpts.markdown: If we could split the fraction into two or more simpler fractions such that their sum is equivalent to the original fraction, we could then proceed by differentiating each of these simpler expressions.
excerpts.why: States the motive for partial fractions: replace one hard differentiation by several easy ones.

excerpts.latex: But it is important to bear in mind that all which follows applies only to what are called ``proper'' algebraic fractions, meaning fractions like the above, which have the numerator of \emph{a lesser degree} than the denominator; that is, those in which the highest index of~$x$ is less in the numerator than in the denominator.
excerpts.markdown: But it is important to bear in mind that all which follows applies only to what are called “proper” algebraic fractions, meaning fractions like the above, which have the numerator of *a lesser degree* than the denominator; that is, those in which the highest index of $x$ is less in the numerator than in the denominator.
excerpts.why: Warns learners when the method applies and when to divide first.

excerpts.latex: The equation must be true for all values of~$x$; therefore it must be true for such values of~$x$ as will cause $x-1$ and~$x+1$ to become zero, that is for $x=1$ and for $x=-1$ respectively.
excerpts.markdown: The equation must be true for all values of $x$; therefore it must be true for such values of $x$ as will cause $x-1$ and $x+1$ to become zero, that is for $x=1$ and for $x=-1$ respectively.
excerpts.why: Explains the key trick that gets round having two unknowns and only one equation.

excerpts.latex: We see that it is sufficient to allow for one numerical term in each numerator, and that we always get the ultimate partial fractions.
excerpts.markdown: We see that it is sufficient to allow for one numerical term in each numerator, and that we always get the ultimate partial fractions.
excerpts.why: Settles a common doubt about repeated factors after the book's own Ax+B attempt failed.

excerpts.latex: It is useful to check the results obtained. The simplest way is to replace $x$ by a single value, say~$+1$, both in the given expression and in the partial fractions obtained.
excerpts.markdown: It is useful to check the results obtained. The simplest way is to replace $x$ by a single value, say $+1$, both in the given expression and in the partial fractions obtained.
excerpts.why: Gives learners a quick habit for catching algebra slips.

excerpts.latex: It follows that, being given a function, if it be easier to differentiate the inverse function, this may be done, and the reciprocal of the differential coefficient of the inverse function gives the differential coefficient of the given function itself.
excerpts.markdown: It follows that, being given a function, if it be easier to differentiate the inverse function, this may be done, and the reciprocal of the differential coefficient of the inverse function gives the differential coefficient of the given function itself.
excerpts.why: States the inverse-function dodge as a practical rule.

excerpts.latex: You will surely realize from this chapter and the preceding, that in many respects the calculus is an \emph{art} rather than a \emph{science}: an art only to be acquired, as all other arts are, by practice.
excerpts.markdown: You will surely realize from this chapter and the preceding, that in many respects the calculus is an *art* rather than a *science*: an art only to be acquired, as all other arts are, by practice.
excerpts.why: Encourages learners to see skill in calculus as built by practice.

excerpts.location: On true Compound Interest and the Law of Organic Growth
excerpts.latex: It is easy to see that if the value of the yearly interest is $\dfrac{1}{n}$~of the capital, he must go on hoarding for $n$~years in order to double his property.
excerpts.markdown: It is easy to see that if the value of the yearly interest is $\dfrac{1}{n}$ of the capital, he must go on hoarding for $n$ years in order to double his property.
excerpts.why: It shows a learner, in the plainest case, how a fixed yearly increment builds up linearly, which sets up the contrast with compound growth.

excerpts.location: On true Compound Interest and the Law of Organic Growth
excerpts.latex: Another reason why $\epsilon$ is important is because it was made by Napier, the inventor of logarithms, the basis of his system.
excerpts.markdown: Another reason why $\epsilon$ is important is because it was made by Napier, the inventor of logarithms, the basis of his system.
excerpts.why: It places Euler's number historically with John Napier and explains why it became the base of natural logarithms.

excerpts.location: On true Compound Interest and the Law of Organic Growth
excerpts.latex: To this mysterious number $2.7182818$ etc., the mathematicians have assigned as a symbol the Greek letter~$\epsilon$ (pronounced \emph{epsilon}). All schoolboys know that the Greek letter~$\pi$ (called \emph{pi}) stands for $3.141592$ etc.; but how many of them know that \emph{epsilon} means $2.71828$? Yet it is an even more important number than~$\pi$!
excerpts.markdown: To this mysterious number $2.7182818$ etc., the mathematicians have assigned as a symbol the Greek letter $\epsilon$ (pronounced *epsilon*). All schoolboys know that the Greek letter $\pi$ (called *pi*) stands for $3.141592$ etc.; but how many of them know that *epsilon* means $2.71828$? Yet it is an even more important number than $\pi$!
excerpts.why: Introduces epsilon with a playful comparison to pi, so learners feel its importance.

excerpts.location: On true Compound Interest and the Law of Organic Growth
excerpts.latex: Suppose we were to let $1$ grow at simple interest till it became~$2$; then, if at the same nominal rate of interest, and for the same time, we were to let $1$ grow at true compound interest, instead of simple, it would grow to the value \emph{epsilon}.
excerpts.markdown: Suppose we were to let $1$ grow at simple interest till it became $2$; then, if at the same nominal rate of interest, and for the same time, we were to let $1$ grow at true compound interest, instead of simple, it would grow to the value *epsilon*.
excerpts.why: Gives a concrete way to understand epsilon by comparing simple and compound growth.

excerpts.location: On true Compound Interest and the Law of Organic Growth
excerpts.latex: But this mode of reckoning compound interest once a year, is really not quite fair; for even during the first year the~£$100$ ought to have been growing. At the end of half a year it ought to have been at least~£$105$, and it certainly would have been fairer had the interest for the second half of the year been calculated on~£$105$.
excerpts.markdown: But this mode of reckoning compound interest once a year, is really not quite fair; for even during the first year the £$100$ ought to have been growing. At the end of half a year it ought to have been at least £$105$, and it certainly would have been fairer had the interest for the second half of the year been calculated on £$105$.
excerpts.why: Motivates compounding more and more often by an intuitive appeal to fairness, the first step toward the limit.

excerpts.location: On true Compound Interest and the Law of Organic Growth
excerpts.latex: This process of growing proportionately, at every instant, to the magnitude at that instant, some people call \emph{a logarithmic rate} of growing. Unit logarithmic rate of growth is that rate which in unit time will cause $1$ to grow to $2.718281$.
excerpts.markdown: This process of growing proportionately, at every instant, to the magnitude at that instant, some people call *a logarithmic rate* of growing. Unit logarithmic rate of growth is that rate which in unit time will cause $1$ to grow to $2.718281$.
excerpts.why: Names the growth process in which size and rate of increase stay proportional.

excerpts.location: On true Compound Interest and the Law of Organic Growth
excerpts.latex: The great reason why $\epsilon$ is regarded of importance is that $\epsilon^x$ possesses a property, not possessed by any other function of~$x$, that \emph{when you differentiate it its value remains unchanged}\Pagelabel{unchanged}; or, in other words, its differential coefficient is the same as itself.
excerpts.markdown: The great reason why $\epsilon$ is regarded of importance is that $\epsilon^x$ possesses a property, not possessed by any other function of $x$, that *when you differentiate it its value remains unchanged*unchanged; or, in other words, its differential coefficient is the same as itself.
excerpts.why: States the single property that makes epsilon^x central to calculus.

excerpts.location: On true Compound Interest and the Law of Organic Growth
excerpts.latex: Note that $x^{-1}$ is a result that we could never have got by the rule for differentiating powers.
excerpts.markdown: Note that $x^{-1}$ is a result that we could never have got by the rule for differentiating powers.
excerpts.why: Warns that the derivative of the logarithm falls outside the power rule, preparing for integration.

excerpts.location: On true Compound Interest and the Law of Organic Growth
excerpts.latex: In fact $\epsilon^{-at}$ serves as a \emph{die-away factor} for all those phenomena in which the rate of decrease is proportional to the magnitude of that which is decreasing; or where, in our usual symbols, $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$~is proportional at every moment to the value that~$y$ has at that moment.
excerpts.markdown: In fact $\epsilon^{-at}$ serves as a *die-away factor* for all those phenomena in which the rate of decrease is proportional to the magnitude of that which is decreasing; or where, in our usual symbols, $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$ is proportional at every moment to the value that $y$ has at that moment.
excerpts.why: Links one formula to cooling, leaking charge and fading oscillations.

excerpts.location: On true Compound Interest and the Law of Organic Growth
excerpts.latex: For the benefit of those who have no tutor at hand it may be of use to state that $\epsilon^x$ is read as ``\emph{epsilon to the eksth power};'' or some people read it ``\emph{exponential eks}.''
excerpts.markdown: For the benefit of those who have no tutor at hand it may be of use to state that $\epsilon^x$ is read as “*epsilon to the eksth power*;” or some people read it “*exponential eks*.”
excerpts.why: A charming aside on how to say exponentials aloud, from a book written for self-teachers.

excerpts.location: How to deal with Sines and Cosines
excerpts.latex: What we have to investigate is the value of $\dfrac{d(\sin \theta)}{d \theta}$; or, in other words, if the angle~$\theta$ varies, we have to find the relation between the increment of the sine and the increment of the angle, both increments being indefinitely small in themselves.
excerpts.markdown: What we have to investigate is the value of $\dfrac{d(\sin \theta)}{d \theta}$; or, in other words, if the angle $\theta$ varies, we have to find the relation between the increment of the sine and the increment of the angle, both increments being indefinitely small in themselves.
excerpts.why: It states plainly what the derivative of the sine means: how a small change in the sine follows from a small change in the angle.

Other names for the quadratic mean of any quantity are its “virtual” value, or its “r.m.s.” (meaning root-mean-square) value. The French term is *valeur efficace*.
excerpts.why: It defines the quadratic mean in words, gives its other names, and links the calculus to alternating currents.

excerpts.markdown: A great part of the labour of integrating things consists in licking them into some shape that can be integrated.
